intro: This is the first of Satie’s three Gymnopédies, marked “Lent et douloureux”. A low bass note is followed by a chord on the second beat while the melody moves slowly above, and one note is changed at the end.

sections.label: A · Bass, chord, then melody
sections.mNote: Bass notes G and D alternate beneath seventh chords.

sections.label: B · Low E, then D minor
sections.mNote: The melody holds E while the chords beneath it change.

sections.label: A · Opening bass accompaniment again
sections.mNote: Four bars of accompaniment come before the melody again

sections.label: B′ · F♮ in the closing phrase
sections.mNote: The final chord closes in D minor.

relations.label: The opening music returns
relations.basis: The piece makes two large statements with different endings. The 87.5 s offset agrees with the return near 88 s, and the matched excerpt covers the repeated body rather than certifying the altered close. CENS diagonal mean 0.939, sustained 53.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 87.5 s (cache/form/satie-gymnopedie-1.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening accompaniment and first phrase
cues.text: The bass sounds on beat one, the chord on beat two. G major seventh alternates with D major seventh, softly and evenly. The melody enters after four bars, and its first phrase ends on an F♯ held for four more bars.
cues.evidence: Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, Dover reprint of the original edition, transcribed by Evin Robertson for Mutopia: bars 1–12. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Held E, bars 19–21
cues.text: In bars 19–21 the melody falls to a low E, tied across three bars. Beneath it the harmony moves from E minor to E minor seventh, then to D minor. The bass still sounds on the first beat and the chord on the second.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 19–21: tied melodic E over bass E–E–D and the accompanying notes G–B, G–B–D, F–A–D. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First ending
cues.text: The closing phrase rises to G, then falls to F♯. After the repeated bass notes, two full chords end the first half, A minor seventh and then D major.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, first ending, bars 32–39. These bar numbers follow Mutopia’s compact repeat notation. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening
cues.text: The low G returns. For four bars the piano plays only bass notes and soft chords, as at the beginning. The melody starts again on the same F♯ and A, and the changed ending comes later.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 1–5 on their second occurrence. The repeat covers bars 1–31 before the second ending. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second ending in D minor
cues.text: The closing phrase reaches G again. This time the melody falls to F♮ while the bass holds E beneath it. The final chord is D minor.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, second ending, bars 40–47: G–F♮ in the melody, E in the bass through bar 45, and D–F♮–A in the final chord. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The melody drops to E
transitions.to: B · Low E, then D minor
transitions.how: The bass leaves its alternating G and D for F♯, B and E. Above the E-minor chord, the melody drops to a low E and holds it through three bars. G major over E follows, then D minor under the same melody note. The slow three-beat accompaniment keeps the rhythm it has had from the start.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 17–21: bass F♯–B–E–E–D and the tied melodic E. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: D major, then the low G
transitions.from: B · Low E, then D minor
transitions.how: A minor seventh closes onto D major, with F♯ in the upper chord. The low G then restarts the accompaniment, and B–D–F♯ enters on beat two to make a G major seventh. D major seventh follows. The melody rests for four bars before it returns.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 38–39 and the second occurrence of bars 1–5. The original writes out the return; Mutopia uses a repeat sign. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: Second ending over an E bass
transitions.to: B′ · F♮ in the closing phrase
transitions.how: The repeated passage ends on D seventh. E minor follows, with G in the melody, as at the first ending. F♮ now replaces the earlier F♯, and D-minor notes sound above an E bass held for six bars. The last two chords are A minor seventh and D minor.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription: bar 31 on its second occurrence, then bars 40–47; compare the first ending, bars 32–39. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

composer.epithet: Composer of the Gymnopédies, who asked pianists to prepare for 840 repetitions with ‘serious immobilities’.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; returned to study at the Schola Cantorum in 1905, aged thirty-nine
Honfleur, then Montmartre; a room in Arcueil from 1898 until his death
Cocteau, Picasso and Massine for Parade; Picabia and René Clair for Relâche
Piano miniatures, songs, ballets, Socrate and the comic Memoirs of an Amnesiac
composer.background:
In April 1912 Erik Satie told the readers of the Revue musicale S.I.M. that he preferred measuring sounds to hearing them. He reported the results of his equipment. A B♭ examined through a phonoscope was so repulsive that he called his servant to look at it; an ordinary F♯, emitted by a large tenor, weighed ninety-three kilograms. “I get more pleasure from measuring a sound than from hearing it,” he wrote. The essay belonged to his Memoirs of an Amnesiac.

He was born in Honfleur in 1866, the son of a French shipping broker and an English mother of Scottish descent. After she died in 1872, he and his brother returned from Paris to their paternal grandparents in Normandy. A local organist, Gustave Vinot, taught him music and introduced him to plainchant. Back in Paris, Satie entered the Conservatoire in 1879. Two periods of study there produced poor reports and no diploma.
